Q: How do I fix INVALID_ALIAS_KEY when trying to transfer a fungible token with a Hedera smart contract? A: 
INVALID_ALIAS_KEY on Hedera usually means
you're passing an EVM address that hasn't
been auto-created on Hedera yet.

Hedera distinguishes between:
→ Native Hedera accounts (0.0.XXXXX)
→ EVM alias accounts (auto-created
  on first HBAR receive)

The fix depends on your transfer method:

1. Use AccountId.fromEvmAddress():
AccountId.fromEvmAddress(0, 0, evmAddress)
← This resolves alias correctly

2. If using HTS precompile in Solidity:
// Wrong — passing raw EVM address
IHederaTokenService.transferToken(
  token, from, to, amount
);

// Right — ensure account exists first
// by checking via mirror node API:
// GET /api/v1/accounts/{evmAddress}
// If 404 → account not yet created

3. Auto-create the account first:
Send a small HBAR amount to the
EVM address before token transfer.
This triggers auto-account creation
on Hedera.

4. Check your token association:
Account must be associated with
the token before receiving it:
IHederaTokenService.associateToken(
  account, token
)

Share your contract code and which
precompile you're using — happy to
look at the specific issue.

Q: Solidity by Nomic Foundation extension only shows errors when typing manually, but fails/freezes on large copy-paste in VS Code (Foundry) A: 
This is a known limitation of the Nomic 
Foundation language server — it uses 
incremental document sync which only 
triggers re-analysis on text change events, 
not bulk paste insertions in some cases.

Quick fixes to try:

1. Force re-evaluation after paste:
   Add a single space anywhere then 
   delete it. This triggers an incremental 
   change event and forces LSP re-analysis.

2. Add to .vscode/settings.json:
{
  "solidity.lsp.enabled": true,
  "[solidity]": {
    "editor.formatOnSave": true
  }
}

3. Switch document sync mode:
{
  "solidity.languageServer
    .documentSync": "full"
}
   Full sync re-analyzes entire document
   on every change instead of incremental.
   Slower but catches paste issues.

4. If still failing:
   Try forge build after paste —
   if it compiles clean, the issue is
   purely LSP not forge itself.

Root cause: incremental sync misses
large paste events as "single change."
Full sync mode usually fixes this.

Q: How to delete from a sorted array without O(n) A:

With a regular sorted array, O(n) deletion is unavoidable.

Binary search only helps you find the element quickly (O(log n)). After that, the array still has to shift all the elements that come after it to fill the gap and keep everything in order. That's why deletion is O(n).

So it's really just one of the trade-offs of using an array:

  • Fast searches with binary search.

  • Slower insertions and deletions because elements need to be shifted.

If you're thinking about using a Set, it's a good option for fast insertions and deletions (average O(1)). However, a Set doesn't keep elements sorted or support binary search, so it solves a different problem.

If your application needs to keep the data sorted and perform lots of inserts and deletes efficiently, it's probably worth looking at a different data structure, such as a balanced tree or a skip list, instead of an array.

Q: Nested dictionary output A:

I'm assuming you're using this package (not totally sure since your code doesn't quite look like the code shown here). Therefore, I'm looking at the structure shown near the bottom of this page. Because this dictionary has inconsistent structure, it will be difficult to iterate through in one clean loop. But since you know the structure and the key names, you can pull out what you want by just using the names of the keys and iterating through each list/dictionary you want to look at individually.

For example, getting the dict for every TCP connection, then iterating through those dictionaries:

tcp_nested_dict = results[ip]["tcp"]

#translates to: for key, value in dict, but renamed for clarity
#the key is the port id
for port_id, info_dict in tcp_nested_dict:
    for key, value in info_dict:
        #your code here

Please note that this code won't work for going through every item in the results dict. For example, it won't work for results[ip]["portused"], because that corresponds to a list of dicts, not another dict.

If you want to go through everything at once, it might be possible with iterators, but it'd be real fussy since this data structure isn't consistently organized. I don't think I would recommend this. There isn't that much stuff in the dictionary, and it's all clearly labeled, so just access the labels you want by using the key names. This will also be more legible.

NOTE: You might not need to use the nested dict at all. It seems like you can also get the nm info as a csv, like this:

nm = nmap.PortScanner()
nm.scan(ip)
print(nm.csv()) #this will just print the csv so you can see it -- eventually, you will probably want to save it or put it into a dataframe.

If the goal is to extract information and save it, this latter option is probably the better choice. But it would depend on exactly what info you wanted and what format you wanted it in.

Q: How to implement a social media/website monitoring service? A:

Just focusing on this:

Review sites I looked at some review site's TOS and they wrote that using an automated software crawling their sites is not permitted.

If the TOS says "no crawling", then you shouldn't do that. They would be within their rights to block you / your company from accessing their sites if you violate their TOS. And they may have other remedies!

Note that there are many reasons for banning crawling. One of them is that crawlers cost them money ... for no return to them.)

A "get out" would be if what you are proposing doesn't violate the review site's TOS. For example, if you could use a (hypothetical) review site APIs to find references to your products ... without "crawling" ... that might be acceptable. However that would depend on 1) the precise wording of the TOS, and 2) what you were actually doing and how you were doing it.

Note that we can't give you sound advice on this. It is fundamentally a legal question. Ask an Intellectual Property lawyer. (We aren't lawyers here!!)

On the other hand, the sites that are relevant to me are not disallowed in their robots.txt. What matters here?

  1. The meaning of the robots.txt file is conventional. It has no legal authority.

  2. It depends on what the robots.txt file says. For example, the file could allow some agents and not others.

  3. If there was an apparent contradiction between a site's TOS and their robots.txt, it may be up to a judge and/or jury to decide which one is operative. But you don't want to get to that point because it will cost your company a lot of money (lawyers fees, discovery costs, etc) to fight a civil lawsuit ... even if you win.

In short, BOTH the TOS and the robots.txt matter. If EITHER says don't crawl, then don't crawl. (Unless you / your company is willing to risk an expensive lawsuit. And if you / they are, then talk to your lawyer first!!)
